newsitem.title: FRANCE: Seguin fires euro thunderbolt into French campaign.
newsitem.headline: Seguin fires euro thunderbolt into French campaign.

text.p: Maverick French Gaullist Philippe Seguin distanced himself from the centre-right government's election platform on Tuesday, denouncing what he called the ultra-liberal logic of European monetary union.

The outgoing National Assembly speaker urged voters to give President Jacques Chirac a parliamentary majority in a snap election on May 25 and June 1, but set himself sharply apart from Prime Minister Alain Juppe's programme.
Denouncing what he called the hollowness of the campaign, Seguin said the fight against unemployment should be the central issue and denounced conventional conservative economic thinking.

Seguin, who spearheaded the campaign against the Maastricht Treaty in a 1992 French referendum, said the forces taking control of the global economy were "totally indifferent to the fate of the people".
"They impose an ultra-liberal logic which serves their immediate interests. Wherever the political authorities cave in, financial logic sweeps away everything in its wake," he said.
Seguin said the European Union had "too often played the good schoolboy of ultra-liberalism. It has seemed to make social disintegration the sole response to the problem".
The Maastricht Treaty was "intrinsically asocial, not to say antisocial (because it) deliberately ignores unemployment and makes the currency not a means but an end in itself", he said.

The speech appeared to reflect both Seguin's isolation on the right, and his disenchantment with the turn of government policy towards free-marketeering deregulation, two years after Chirac was elected promising to heal France's social fracture.
Parliamentary sources said he had opposed Chirac's decision to dissolve parliament early and warned against subjugating the fight against unemployment to deficit cutting.

Seguin accused the opposition Socialist Party of hypocrisy for raising reservations now about strict observance of the criteria for a single European currency, recalling that a Socialist government negotiated the Maastricht treaty.
"It was the Socialists who signed this ultra-liberal capitulation. They were the ones who began the decline in social solidarity," he declared.

In an assault on the centre-right's mainstream political credo, Seguin lamented that in response to rising unemployment, "people everywhere are repeating words that seem meaningless: convergence criteria, flexibility, globalisation, federalism."
He said such slogans were "alibis for inaction disguised as promises of a radiant future".
